title: Hungarian Beef Goulash with Potatoes and Peppers
summary: Chunks of beef chuck are browned, then simmered slowly with onions, paprika and caraway until tender, before potatoes and peppers are added to finish into a thick, warming stew.
equipment: large heavy casserole (Dutch oven, 6 litres) with lid

ingredients.item: beef chuck (stewing beef), trimmed, cut into 3 cm cubes
hot paprika or a pinch of cayenne
fine sea salt or table salt
waxy potatoes, peeled, cut into 3 cm chunks
red pepper, cut into 3 cm pieces
yellow pepper, cut into 3 cm pieces

steps.title: Brown the beef
steps.text: Pat the beef dry, then heat the oil in the casserole over medium-high heat and brown the beef in 2-3 batches, without crowding the pan, for 5-6 minutes per batch. Set the browned beef aside; browning in batches keeps the pan hot enough for a proper crust to form, which adds flavour that plain boiling never would.

steps.title: Cook the onions
steps.text: Lower the heat to medium, add the onions to the casserole and cook for 12-15 minutes, stirring and scraping the base often, until soft and golden. Add the garlic and caraway and cook for a further 1 minute. Slow-cooked onions essentially melt into the finished sauce, giving it body and a natural sweetness.

steps.title: Add the paprika
steps.text: Take the casserole off the heat and stir in both paprikas and the tomato purée for 30 seconds, then immediately add the stock, water, bay leaves, salt, pepper and the browned beef with its juices. Paprika scorches and turns bitter if it sits over direct heat for too long, so it needs to go in off the heat and be followed quickly by the liquid.

steps.title: Simmer the beef
steps.text: Bring the pot to the boil, then cover and simmer very gently for 1 hour 30 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the beef is nearly tender. A bare simmer rather than a vigorous boil keeps the tough chuck beef cooking gently enough to break down without the liquid boiling away too fast.

steps.title: Add the vegetables
steps.text: Add the potatoes and peppers and simmer, partly covered, for 30-40 minutes, until the beef is fully tender and the potatoes are cooked through and starting to thicken the broth. The starch released from the potatoes naturally thickens the sauce as it finishes cooking.

steps.title: Finish and serve
steps.text: Stir in the vinegar and remove the bay leaves, then serve the goulash in bowls with crusty bread. The splash of vinegar at the end sharpens all the rich, slow-cooked flavours without needing extra salt.

tips: Brown the beef in small batches rather than all at once; overcrowding the pan stops it browning properly and the beef ends up grey and steamed instead.
Add the paprika off the heat and get the liquid in quickly afterwards — paprika burns and turns bitter if it sits in a hot, dry pan.
Keep the stew at a bare simmer rather than a rolling boil during the long cooking time; this breaks down the tough chuck beef without toughening it further.
Don't add the potatoes and peppers at the start — they'll turn to mush over the long simmer needed to tenderise the beef.
safety: Cool leftovers within 2 hours of cooking rather than leaving the pot to cool on the side for longer, to keep it safe to store.
storage: Cool leftovers within 2 hours, then refrigerate in a covered container for up to 3 days. Reheat in a pan over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until piping hot throughout (74°C); this goulash also freezes well for up to 3 months.
